one_liner: Arena-backed, span-preserving Rust TOML 1.1 library; parses ~9x and parse+deserializes ~3x faster than the `toml` crate.
what_it_does: A complete TOML 1.1 library. `parse(&str, &Arena)` returns a `Document` tree in which every value carries a byte span into the source. Index operators (`doc["a"][0]["b"]`) return a None-like `MaybeItem` instead of panicking. Typed conversion uses its own `FromToml`/`ToToml` traits and a zero-dependency `#[derive(Toml)]` macro instead of serde, and errors accumulate with spans and TOML paths rather than stopping at the first one. It also writes TOML and can keep the comments, whitespace and ordering of a previously parsed document; it started as a fork of EmbarkStudios' toml-span but has been almost entirely rewritten.
how_it_is_fast: All tree nodes are allocated in a bump arena, and strings without escapes are borrowed zero-copy from the input, so parsing makes very few individual heap allocations. `Item` is 24 bytes: the type tag, container flags and span are bit-packed into two u32s. Tables are flat vectors kept in insertion order and searched linearly; once a table reaches 6 entries, one foldhash index for the whole parse, keyed on (the table's first-key offset, key), takes over, and `TableHelper` deserialization reuses that index and tracks consumed fields in a bitset. String bodies are scanned 8 bytes at a time with SWAR (SIMD-within-a-register) bit tricks to find delimiters, backslashes and control bytes; the changelog also credits pointer traversal, batched string reads and reduced LLVM IR.
when_to_use: Rust tools that load TOML configs or manifests on a startup or hot path (CLIs, build tools, dev servers), where `toml` parse time is visible. On real Cargo.toml and tool config files the README shows ~9x faster parsing.

Linters, language servers and config validators that need exact source locations. Every parsed value keeps a byte span, and errors carry spans plus TOML paths and render through annotate-snippets or codespan-reporting.
Reporting every config mistake in one pass. Conversion errors accumulate in the `Document` context, and `parse_recoverable` continues past syntax errors (up to 25) instead of failing on the first.

Rewriting user-edited TOML while keeping comments and layout (`Formatting::preserved_from`), as a lighter option than toml_edit, which took ~12x longer to parse zed/Cargo.toml in the same table (306.6 vs 24.5 us).

Crates that care about build time or binary size. For a simplified Cargo.toml model, the author's separate build benchmark reports a 52 ms warm `cargo check` vs 169 ms for toml, and a 204 KB vs 500 KB stripped release binary.
when_not_to_use: Codebases built on serde `Deserialize`: `toml::from_str` call sites and serde-derived types must be ported to `#[derive(Toml)]` or hand-written `FromToml`. The `serde` feature only adds `Serialize` impls for `Item`/`Spanned`.
Workloads dominated by deserialization. The author calls the deserialization gains 'marginal', and the end-to-end lead over toml falls to 2.9x (Cargo.lock) and 3.3x (Cargo.toml).
Documents of 256 MiB or more. They are rejected with `FileTooLarge` because spans are 28-bit.
Dependency policies that forbid or strictly audit `unsafe`. The arena, packed items and tables rely heavily on unsafe code, and its safety rests on the author's Miri runs and fuzzing.

Risk-averse production use: the project is young (first release January 2026, 1.0 in March 2026) and has a small user base (33 stars, ~38.6k crates.io downloads, 6 reverse dependencies). `toml` is the ecosystem standard.

integration.dependencies: foldhash (required); optional: serde (Serialize impls), zmij (float formatting, enabled by `to-toml`), toml-spanner-macros (`derive` feature; the macro crate itself has no dependencies)
integration.min_toolchain: Rust 1.90 (edition 2024); the derive macro crate declares 1.84
integration.platforms: any: pure Rust with portable u64 SWAR and no arch-specific SIMD; 32-bit (i686) is tested under Miri
integration.thread_safety: Parsed `Item`/`Table`/`Array` and `OwnedItem`/`OwnedTable` are Send + Sync (since 1.0.2). `Arena` is Send but not Sync because its bump pointers are `Cell`s, so allocate from one thread at a time (one arena per parse or thread).
integration.drop_in_for_baseline: partial: the API is different. `parse(&str, &Arena)` returns a `Document` that borrows from the arena, and typed deserialization goes through `FromToml`/`#[derive(Toml)]` rather than serde `Deserialize`. A `toml_spanner::from_str` exists but requires `T: FromToml`. Tables keep insertion order by default, unlike `toml` without `preserve_order`.

gotchas: The `Document` borrows both the input `&str` and the `Arena`. To keep parsed data past their lifetimes, convert it to your own types or use `OwnedItem`/`OwnedTable` (added in 1.0.2).
`Table::get` and `doc["key"]` scan linearly. The foldhash index speeds up only parsing and `TableHelper` extraction, so ad-hoc lookups on very wide tables are O(n).
`parse` rejects inputs of 1<<28 bytes (256 MiB) or more, but the `ErrorKind::FileTooLarge` docs and error message say 512 MiB.

Integers are stored as i128, so values outside the i64 range, which `toml` rejects, are accepted. The project's fuzz comparison against toml skips these as a known divergence; check with `as_i64` if you need 64-bit range.
pick_this_over_siblings_when: It is the only Rust library among the catalogued TOML parsers, so pick it for Rust code. teptris (C, vs toml++), TOMLDecoder (Swift) and go-toml v2 (Go) serve other languages and were measured against different baselines, so their speedups cannot be compared with this one.
verified_claims_summary: These are the author's own cycle/instruction-counter benchmarks on an AMD Ryzen 9 5950X (Linux 6.18). The README states rustc 1.94.1, but the repo's benchmark action runs `cargo +nightly run --release` with the default release profile and no LTO. toml-spanner 1.0.0 parsed zed/Cargo.toml in 24.5 us vs 228.5 us for toml 1.0.7 parsing into `toml::Table` with `fast_hash` on (~9.3x), and was 8.8-9.7x faster on two smaller configs. With deserialization into cargo's own lockfile/manifest types included, the lead shrinks to 2.9x (Cargo.lock, 1023.5 vs 2977.4 us) and 3.3x (Cargo.toml, 92.5 vs 309.4 us); none of this has been independently reproduced.
status_note: Actively maintained (1.0.3 released 2026-06-17, one open issue), dual MIT/Apache-2.0, pure Rust with a single required dependency, so it is easy to adopt, but it is young and lightly used.
